source.title: Enhanced Response Envelope via Envelope Regularization

record.tranche_reason: Tests the general double-descent pattern in a multivariate linear envelope model using asymptotic risk analysis and simulations, rather than reproducing the original deep-network method.
record.gate_note: The study reports a limiting risk curve and simulated prediction-risk curves for the envelope estimator as p/n varies. It does not test epochs or increasing sample size near interpolation. Results from cited work are not recorded as rows; fixed-ratio estimator comparisons are not rows for the double-descent curve.
record.test_reason: The study derives the limiting prediction risk of an envelope linear-regression estimator as p/n varies (Theorem 2). It also simulates risk curves over p/n from 0.1 to 5. Both show risk rising up to p/n = 1 and falling after it. This is a new model class and setting with its own result on the general double-descent curve (V4), so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that asymptotic risk analysis reveals double descent for the envelope estimator and that simulations confirm it, including with correlated predictors. Their main conclusion is that the enhanced response envelope always has lower risk than the envelope, with the largest gains near p ≈ n.
record.recipe_differences: Studies prediction risk for an envelope regression estimator, not deep networks; uses high-dimensional asymptotic analysis and simulations over p/n.
record.peer_reviewed: Journal of the American Statistical Association
record.problems: The reported simulated double-descent curves are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. The tested setting is a particular envelope regression model.

untested.parts: No deep networks; capacity here is the number of linear predictors.
Sample size is never varied at fixed p. Theorem 2 implies more data raises risk for γ > 1, but the authors do not examine or state this.
No effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested across axes.
Label noise and multiple peaks are not studied. The study does not state whether the optimally tuned enhanced estimator (λ*) removes the peak; see missing.

missing.what: Numeric envelope risk (true u) across p/n, rising then falling. For n = 200, ρ = 0: about 1.3 at 0.1, 4.7 at 0.3, 115 at 0.9, 95 at 1.1, 11.9 at 3, 10.5 at 10. The pattern is similar for other n and ρ.

Limiting risk of the enhanced (ridge-type) envelope at the oracle-tuned λ* = tr(Ω)γ/c². It lies below the envelope curve and shows no peak at γ = 1 in Figure 1. The text does not explicitly say whether the peak disappears, and λ* uses the true parameters.
With cross-validated u, the envelope estimator's peak largely vanishes: risk about 10 at p/n = 0.9 versus 113–162 with true u. This is a model-selection effect.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The main aim is a new regularized estimator; double descent is a secondary theoretical result. Theorem 2 assumes a known envelope subspace and Σx = I, while the simulations estimate the subspace. The 'double descent' here is rise-then-fall with no initial descent, and the second descent tends to the null risk rather than beating the low-p risk.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps and the peak near the training-set interpolation threshold.
Changing sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests the pattern in an envelope regression model, not across a broad range of model classes.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Noise dependence, multiple or split peaks, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Whether effective parameter counting turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Envelope estimator
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed limiting prediction risk as p/n converges to γ.
rows.value: For γ < 1: tr(Ω)γ/(1−γ). For γ > 1: c²(1−1/γ) + tr(Ω)/(γ−1). The authors state that limiting risk increases before γ = 1 and decreases after γ = 1.
rows.note: The paper identifies the rise before γ = 1 and descent after γ = 1 as double descent.
rows.check: Correct as recorded, but the shape lacks a first descent. For γ < 1 the risk rises monotonically from 0 because bias is zero, so there is no classical U. As γ → ∞ the risk tends to the null risk c², never below the small-γ risk.

relationships.condition: Envelope estimator (known subspace, asymptotic, Σx = I) and simulated envelope estimator with u = 2, n = 200 or 2000, ρ = 0 or 0.8
relationships.reason: Limiting risk diverges as γ → 1 and decreases for γ > 1 (R1). Simulated curves show the same rise and second descent past p/n = 1 (R2–R5). Table 1–3 numbers (not yet rows) confirm this. The second descent only approaches the null risk c².
relationships.display_finding: Theoretical risk diverged as γ→1 and declined for γ>1, matching simulated second descents beyond p/n=1 and approaching the null risk c².
